newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong leadership hopeful outlines platform.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong leadership hopeful outlines platform.

text.p: The latest candidate to throw his hat into the ring to lead Hong Kong when the British leave next year sought to steal a march on his nearest rivals on Tuesday by declaring his policy platform.

Peter Woo, who announced on Monday he would seek to succeed Governor Chris Patten when British rule draws to a close at midnight on June 30, 1997, was the first of those tipped as the front runners to outline his ideas for governing the wealthy but nervous community of six million people.

Woo, a son-in-law of the late Hong Kong shipping magnate Sir Yue-kong Pao, told a news conference that one of his top priorities would be to calm public jitters by establishing a sound government capable of speaking up for its interests after the handover.
In economic terms, his plans differ little from the familiar fiscally prudent policies of the colonial government which advocate balanced budgets and small government.

But if Hong Kong's vocal democratic movement had been hoping for signs Woo intends to build on the limited electoral and social reforms introduced by Patten in the twilight of more than 150 years of British rule, they will be disappointed.

The democrats have freely expressed fears that many of the freedoms, human rights guarantees and the rule of law may be eroded by the same government which cracked down on the democracy demonstrators of Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.

Woo said he planned to establish a two-tier advisory board to consult on public policy and economic strategy and put in place an early-warning system to protect against financial shocks and any speculative run on Hong Kong's currency.
"We must therefore be totally prepared to maintain the stability of our financial system and to ensure international investors and speculators are aware of our solidarity and our resolve," he said.
But in a sign he is leaning toward re-introducing the system of political appointments, Woo said he would seek to appoint community leaders to local government councils.
The democratic reforms spearheaded by Patten, which drove a deep wedge between Britain and China in the delicate countdown years, swept away the traditional colonial appointments system.
In recent years, Woo has turned his back on big business to concentrate on public service.

Shanghai-born Woo remains honorary chairman of blue chips Wharf (Holdings) Ltd and Wheelock and Co Ltd, but stepped back from day-to-day running of his companies to become chairman of Hong Kong's Hospital Authority which runs public infirmaries.
At 50, he is the fifth and youngest candidate to enter the the race for Hong Kong's post-colonial leadership.
Billionaire businessman Tung Chee-hwa, 59, son of a late rival shipping magnate, has also said he is considering joining the fray. He is regarded in Hong Kong as the front runner.
Popularity polls put Patten's deputy Anson Chan, head of Hong Kong's powerful civil service, far ahead of the five contenders, although she has not declared her candidacy.
Popularity is not an issue, however.

Hong Kong's first post-handover leader will be selected in November by a 400-strong body to be appointed by China's handpicked Preparatory Committee charged with transforming the British colony into a Special Administrative Region of China.
